Tuppence opened the door of an empty first-class compartment, and the two girls sank down breathless on the padded seats."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "Tuppence took Jane’s hand in hers. “Tommy wouldn’t have told us to do this unless he was sure we’d be all right.”"}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "“But he doesn’t know them as I do!” The girl shivered. “You can’t understand. Five years! Five long years! Sometimes I thought I should go mad.”"}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“Never mind. It’s all over.”"}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“Is it?”"}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "The train was moving now, speeding through the night."}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“My cousin didn’t think it was safe. He didn’t want us to do this.”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“No,” said Tuppence, rather embarrassed."}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“What are you thinking of?” said Jane sharply. “Your voice was so--queer!”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“I _was_ thinking of something,” confessed Tuppence. “But I don’t want to tell you--not now. I may be wrong, but I don’t think so. It’s just an idea that came into my head a long time ago. Tommy’s got it too--I’m almost sure he has. Lie back and don’t think of anything.”"}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "“I’ll try.” The long lashes drooped over the hazel eyes."}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "Tuppence, for her part, sat bolt upright--much in the attitude of a watchful terrier on guard. In her own mind she was far from feeling the confidence displayed in her words. Not that she disbelieved in Tommy, but occasionally she was shaken with doubts as to whether anyone so simple and honest as he was could ever be a match for the fiendish subtlety of the arch-criminal."}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "Tuppence mapped out her plan of campaign."}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "As the train drew into Charing Cross, Jane sat up with a start."}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“Have we arrived? I never thought we should!”"}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“If there’s going to be any fun, now is when it will begin. Quick, get out. We’ll nip into a taxi.”"}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“King’s Cross,” directed Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“You see,” she explained to Jane, “if they think we’re going to Sir James, this will put them off the scent. Now they’ll imagine we’re going to Mr. Carter.”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "Crossing Holborn there was a block, and the taxi was held up. This was what Tuppence had been waiting for."}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“Quick,” she whispered. “Open the right-hand door!”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "The two girls stepped out into the traffic. Two minutes later they were seated in another taxi, this time bound direct for Carlton House Terrace."}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "“There,” said Tuppence, with great satisfaction, “this ought to do them. I can’t help thinking that I’m really rather clever! What’s this thing swerving----Oh!”"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "There was a grinding noise and a bump. Another taxi had collided with them."}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "In a flash Tuppence was out on the pavement. Before the approaching policeman arrived she had handed the driver five shillings, and she and Jane had merged themselves in the crowd."}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "“It may be my fancy,” said Tuppence suddenly, “but I feel as though there was some one behind us.”"}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "“Hurry!” murmured the other. “Oh, hurry!”"}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "At the corner of Carlton House Terrace a large and apparently intoxicated man barred their way. He clutched Jane by the shoulder. Tuppence heard other footsteps behind. Lowering her head, she repeated a manœuvre of childish days, and butted their aggressor full in the capacious middle. The man sat down abruptly on the pavement. Tuppence and Jane took to their heels, footsteps echoing behind them, and reached Sir James’s door in choking gasps. Tuppence seized the bell and Jane the knocker."}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "The man who had stopped them reached the foot of the steps. For a moment he hesitated, and as he did so the door opened. They fell into the hall together. Sir James came forward from the library door."}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“Hullo! What’s this?”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "He put his arm round Jane as she swayed, half carried her into the library, and laid her on the leather couch. From a tantalus on the table he poured out a few drops of brandy, and forced her to drink them."}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“It’s all right. Don’t be afraid, my child. You’re quite safe.” Sir James looked at Tuppence quizzically. “So you’re not dead, Miss Tuppence, any more than that Tommy boy of yours was! And this”--he turned to the girl on the couch--“is Miss Jane Finn?”"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“Yes,” she said quietly, “I am Jane Finn. I have a lot to tell you.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“When you are stronger----”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“No--now! I shall feel safer when I have told everything.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“As you please,” said the lawyer, and sat down facing the couch. In a low voice Jane began her story."}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "“I came over on the _Lusitania_ to take up a post in a hospital in Paris."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "“When the _Lusitania_ was torpedoed, a man came up to me. He asked me if I was a patriotic American, and told me he was carrying papers which were just life or death to the Allies. He asked me to take charge of them."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“Mr. Danvers had told me to watch out. At first I had no suspicions, but on the boat to Holyhead I began to get uneasy. There was one woman who had been very keen to chum up with me--a Mrs. Vandemeyer. I felt there was something about her I didn’t like, and on the Irish boat I saw her talking to some queer-looking men, and from the way they looked I saw that they were talking about me."}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "“The only thing was to act as though I’d noticed nothing, and hope for the best. One thing I’d done already as a precaution--ripped open the oilskin packet and substituted blank paper, and then sewn it up again."}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "“What to do with the real thing worried me no end. Finally I opened it out flat--there were only two sheets--and laid it between two of the advertisement pages of a magazine. I stuck the two pages together round the edge with some gum off an envelope. I carried the magazine carelessly stuffed into the pocket of my ulster."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“At Holyhead I tried to get into a carriage with people that looked all right. In the end I found myself in a carriage with Mrs. Vandemeyer after all. There was quite a nice-looking man and his wife sitting just opposite, so I felt almost happy about it until just outside London. I had leaned back and closed my eyes. I guess they thought I was asleep, but my eyes weren’t quite shut, and suddenly I saw the nice-looking man get something out of his bag and hand it to Mrs. Vandemeyer, and as he did so he _winked_...."}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "“I can’t tell you how that wink sort of froze me through and through. I got up, trying to look natural and easy. Suddenly Mrs. Vandemeyer said ‘Now,’ and flung something over my nose and mouth as I tried to scream. At the same moment I felt a terrific blow on the back of my head....”"}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "She shuddered. In a minute she resumed:"}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“When I came back to consciousness I was lying on a dirty bed. There was a screen round it, but I could hear two people talking in the room. Mrs. Vandemeyer was one of them."}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“They hadn’t found the papers. They’d got the oilskin packet with the blanks, and they were just mad! They didn’t know whether _I_’d changed the papers, or whether Danvers had been carrying a dummy message. They spoke of”--she closed her eyes--“torturing me to find out!"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“I’d never known what fear--really sickening fear--was before! I knew I wouldn’t be able to stand up against torture very long."}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“Suddenly something put the thought of loss of memory into my head. The subject had always interested me, and I’d read an awful lot about it. If only I could succeed in carrying the bluff through, it might save me. Then I opened my eyes and started babbling in _French!_"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "“Mrs. Vandemeyer came round the screen at once. Her face was so wicked I nearly died, but I smiled up at her doubtfully, and asked her in French where I was."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“It puzzled her, I could see. She called the man she had been talking to. He stood by the screen with his face in shadow. He spoke to me in French. His voice was very ordinary and quiet, but somehow, I don’t know why, he scared me worse than the woman. He asked me my name. I said I didn’t know--that I couldn’t remember anything at all."}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Suddenly he caught my wrist, and began twisting it. The pain was awful. I screamed and screamed, but I managed to shriek out things in French. Luckily I fainted. The last thing I heard was his voice saying: ‘That’s not bluff! Anyway, a kid of her age wouldn’t know enough.’"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“When I came to, Mrs. Vandemeyer was sweet as honey to me. I murmured something about the ‘doctor’ having hurt my wrist."}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“By and by she went out of the room. In the end I got up and walked round, examining it. It was a squalid, dirty place. There were no windows, which seemed queer. There were some battered old pictures on the walls, representing scenes from _Faust_.”"}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "Jane’s two listeners gave a simultaneous “Ah!” The girl nodded."}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“Yes--it was the place in Soho where Mr. Beresford was imprisoned. My heart gave a great throb of relief when I saw my ulster lying carelessly over the back of a chair. _And the magazine was still rolled up in the pocket!_"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "“There didn’t seem to be a peep-hole of any kind--nevertheless I felt kind of sure there must be. All of a sudden I sat down on the edge of the table, and put my face in my hands, sobbing out a ‘Mon Dieu! Mon Dieu!’ I distinctly heard the rustle of a dress, and slight creak. That was enough for me. I was being watched!"}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“By and by Mrs. Vandemeyer brought me some supper. Presently she produced the oilskin packet, and asked me if I recognized it, watching me like a lynx all the time. I turned it over in a puzzled sort of way and shook my head. Then she told me that I was her niece, and that I was to call her ‘Aunt Rita.’ I did obediently."}, {"paragraph": 58, "text": "“They might throw that magazine away any minute. About two o’clock in the morning I got up as softly as I could, and felt in the dark along the left-hand wall. Very gently, I unhooked one of the pictures from its nail--Marguerite with her casket of jewels. I took the magazine from my coat, damped the brown paper at the back of the picture all round, and pulled it away. I slipped the two stuck-together pages with their precious enclosure between the picture and its backing, and a little gum from an envelope helped me to stick it up again. I rehung it, put the magazine back in my coat pocket, and crept back to bed. They’d never think of pulling to pieces one of their own pictures."}, {"paragraph": 59, "text": "“I learnt afterwards that they nearly did away with me then and there--but the first man, who was the boss, preferred to keep me alive on the chance of my having hidden them, and being able to tell where if I recovered my memory."}, {"paragraph": 60, "text": "“They took me back to Ireland, and over every step of the journey again, in case I’d hidden it somewhere _en route_."}, {"paragraph": 61, "text": "“It ended in my being sent to a sanatorium at Bournemouth. A hospital nurse had charge of me. She seemed so nice and normal that at last I determined to confide in her. My door happened to be ajar, and I heard her talking to some one in the passage. _She was one of them!_"}, {"paragraph": 62, "text": "“I think I almost hypnotized myself. After a while, I almost forgot that I was really Jane Finn. I wasn’t even unhappy in the end--just apathetic. And the years went on."}, {"paragraph": 63, "text": "“And then suddenly things seemed to change. There was some talk of sending me to a specialist in Paris. I learnt later that the nurse went to Paris and consulted a specialist, representing herself to be me. He exposed her loss of memory to be fraudulent; but she had taken a note of his methods and reproduced them on me."}, {"paragraph": 64, "text": "“One night I was whisked off to London, back to the house in Soho."}, {"paragraph": 65, "text": "“They sent me in to wait on Mr. Beresford. I was suspicious--I thought it was another trap. But he looked so honest, I could hardly believe it. However, I was careful in all I said, for I knew we could be overheard. There’s a small hole, high up in the wall."}, {"paragraph": 66, "text": "“But on the Sunday afternoon word came that he was to be killed. I thought I’d have time to rush up and get the papers, but I was caught. So I screamed out that he was escaping, and I said I wanted to go back to Marguerite. I shouted the name three times very loud. I knew the others would think I meant Mrs. Vandemeyer, but I hoped it might make Mr. Beresford think of the picture. He’d unhooked one the first day--that’s what made me hesitate to trust him.”"}, {"paragraph": 67, "text": "“Then the papers,” said Sir James slowly, “are still at the back of the picture in that room.”"}, {"paragraph": 68, "text": "“Yes.” The girl sank back on the sofa exhausted."}, {"paragraph": 69, "text": "Sir James rose and looked at his watch."}, {"paragraph": 70, "text": "“Come,” he said, “we must go at once.”"}, {"paragraph": 71, "text": "“To-night?” queried Tuppence, surprised."}, {"paragraph": 72, "text": "“To-morrow may be too late,” said Sir James gravely. “Besides, by going to-night we have the chance of capturing that great man and super-criminal--Mr. Brown! You have been followed here--not a doubt of it. When we leave the house we shall be followed again, but not molested, _for it is Mr. Brown’s plan that we are to lead him_. But the Soho house is under police supervision night and day. When we enter that house, Mr. Brown will not draw back--he will risk all, on the chance of obtaining the spark to fire his mine. And he fancies the risk not great--since he will enter in the guise of a friend!”"}, {"paragraph": 73, "text": "Tuppence flushed, then opened her mouth impulsively."}, {"paragraph": 74, "text": "“But there’s something you don’t know--that we haven’t told you.” Her eyes dwelt on Jane in perplexity. “It’s so difficult--if I’m wrong--oh, it would be dreadful.”"}, {"paragraph": 75, "text": "“You want me to help you out, eh?” Sir James asked."}, {"paragraph": 76, "text": "“Yes, please. _You_ know who Mr. Brown is, don’t you?”"}, {"paragraph": 77, "text": "“Yes,” said Sir James gravely. “At last I do. I have been morally certain of his identity ever since the night of Mrs. Vandemeyer’s mysterious death. Either the chloral was administered by her own hand, which theory I reject utterly, or else it was administered in the brandy you gave her. Only three people touched that brandy--you, Miss Tuppence, I myself, and one other--Mr. Julius Hersheimmer!”"}, {"paragraph": 78, "text": "Jane Finn stirred and sat up, regarding the speaker with wide astonished eyes."}, {"paragraph": 79, "text": "“At first, the thing seemed utterly impossible,” Sir James went on. “But you cannot escape from the logic of facts. I took an early opportunity of giving you a hint. Then Mr. Beresford rang me up and told me, what I had already suspected, that the photograph of Miss Jane Finn had never really been out of Mr. Hersheimmer’s possession----”"}, {"paragraph": 80, "text": "But the girl interrupted. Springing to her feet, she cried out angrily:"}, {"paragraph": 81, "text": "“What do you mean? That Mr. Brown is _Julius?_ Julius--my own cousin!”"}, {"paragraph": 82, "text": "“No, Miss Finn,” said Sir James unexpectedly. “Not your cousin. The man who calls himself Julius Hersheimmer is no relation to you whatsoever.”"}], "028.source": [{"paragraph": 1, "text": "THE supper party given by Mr. Julius Hersheimmer to a few friends on the
evening of the 30th will long be remembered in catering circles. It took
place in a private room, and Mr. Hersheimmer’s orders were brief and
forcible. He gave carte blanche--and when a millionaire gives carte
blanche he usually gets it!"}, {"paragraph": 2, "text": "Every delicacy out of season was duly provided. Waiters carried bottles
of ancient and royal vintage with loving care. The floral decorations
defied the seasons, and fruits of the earth as far apart as May and
November found themselves miraculously side by side. The list of guests
was small and select. The American Ambassador, Mr. Carter, who had taken
the liberty, he said, of bringing an old friend, Sir William Beresford,
with him, Archdeacon Cowley, Dr. Hall, those two youthful adventurers,
Miss Prudence Cowley and Mr. Thomas Beresford, and last, but not least,
as guest of honour, Miss Jane Finn."}, {"paragraph": 3, "text": "Julius had spared no pains to make Jane’s appearance a success. A
mysterious knock had brought Tuppence to the door of the apartment she
was sharing with the American girl. It was Julius. In his hand he held a
cheque."}, {"paragraph": 4, "text": "“Say, Tuppence,” he began, “will you do me a good turn? Take this, and
get Jane regularly togged up for this evening. You’re all coming to
supper with me at the _Savoy_. See? Spare no expense. You get me?”"}, {"paragraph": 5, "text": "“Sure thing,” mimicked Tuppence. “We shall enjoy ourselves. It will be a
pleasure dressing Jane. She’s the loveliest thing I’ve ever seen.”"}, {"paragraph": 6, "text": "“That’s so,” agreed Mr. Hersheimmer fervently."}, {"paragraph": 7, "text": "His fervour brought a momentary twinkle to Tuppence’s eye."}, {"paragraph": 8, "text": "“By the way, Julius,” she remarked demurely, “I--haven’t given you my
answer yet.”"}, {"paragraph": 9, "text": "“Answer?” said Julius. His face paled."}, {"paragraph": 10, "text": "“You know--when you asked me to--marry you,” faltered Tuppence, her
eyes downcast in the true manner of the early Victorian heroine, “and
wouldn’t take no for an answer. I’ve thought it well over----”"}, {"paragraph": 11, "text": "“Yes?” said Julius. The perspiration stood on his forehead."}, {"paragraph": 12, "text": "Tuppence relented suddenly."}, {"paragraph": 13, "text": "“You great idiot!” she said. “What on earth induced you to do it? I
could see at the time you didn’t care a twopenny dip for me!”"}, {"paragraph": 14, "text": "“Not at all. I had--and still have--the highest sentiments of esteem and
respect--and admiration for you----”"}, {"paragraph": 15, "text": "“H’m!” said Tuppence. “Those are the kind of sentiments that very soon
go to the wall when the other sentiment comes along! Don’t they, old
thing?”"}, {"paragraph": 16, "text": "“I don’t know what you mean,” said Julius stiffly, but a large and
burning blush overspread his countenance."}, {"paragraph": 17, "text": "“Shucks!” retorted Tuppence. She laughed, and closed the door, reopening
it to add with dignity: “Morally, I shall always consider I have been
jilted!”"}, {"paragraph": 18, "text": "“What was it?” asked Jane as Tuppence rejoined her."}, {"paragraph": 19, "text": "“Julius.”"}, {"paragraph": 20, "text": "“What did he want?”"}, {"paragraph": 21, "text": "“Really, I think, he wanted to see you, but I wasn’t going to let him.
Not until to-night, when you’re going to burst upon every one like King
Solomon in his glory! Come on! _We’re going to shop!_”"}, {"paragraph": 22, "text": "To most people the 29th, the much-heralded “Labour Day,” had passed much
as any other day. Speeches were made in the Park and Trafalgar Square.
Straggling processions, singing the _Red Flag_, wandered through the
streets in a more or less aimless manner. Newspapers which had hinted at
a general strike, and the inauguration of a reign of terror, were forced
to hide their diminished heads. The bolder and more astute among
them sought to prove that peace had been effected by following their
counsels. In the Sunday papers a brief notice of the sudden death of Sir
James Peel Edgerton, the famous K.C., had appeared. Monday’s paper
dealt appreciatively with the dead man’s career. The exact manner of his
sudden death was never made public."}, {"paragraph": 23, "text": "Tommy had been right in his forecast of the situation. It had been a
one-man show. Deprived of their chief, the organization fell to pieces.
Kramenin had made a precipitate return to Russia, leaving England early
on Sunday morning. The gang had fled from Astley Priors in a panic,
leaving behind, in their haste, various damaging documents which
compromised them hopelessly. With these proofs of conspiracy in their
hands, aided further by a small brown diary taken from the pocket of the
dead man which had contained a full and damning résumé of the whole
plot, the Government had called an eleventh-hour conference. The Labour
leaders were forced to recognize that they had been used as a cat’s
paw. Certain concessions were made by the Government, and were eagerly
accepted. It was to be Peace, not War!"}, {"paragraph": 24, "text": "But the Cabinet knew by how narrow a margin they had escaped utter
disaster. And burnt in on Mr. Carter’s brain was the strange scene which
had taken place in the house in Soho the night before."}, {"paragraph": 25, "text": "He had entered the squalid room to find that great man, the friend of
a lifetime, dead--betrayed out of his own mouth. From the dead man’s
pocket-book he had retrieved the ill-omened draft treaty, and then
and there, in the presence of the other three, it had been reduced to
ashes.... England was saved!"}, {"paragraph": 26, "text": "And now, on the evening of the 30th, in a private room at the _Savoy_,
Mr. Julius P. Hersheimmer was receiving his guests."}, {"paragraph": 27, "text": "Mr. Carter was the first to arrive. With him was a choleric-looking old
gentleman, at sight of whom Tommy flushed up to the roots of his hair.
He came forward."}, {"paragraph": 28, "text": "“Ha!” said the old gentleman, surveying him apoplectically. “So you’re
my nephew, are you? Not much to look at--but you’ve done good work, it
seems. Your mother must have brought you up well after all. Shall we
let bygones be bygones, eh? You’re my heir, you know; and in future I
propose to make you an allowance--and you can look upon Chalmers Park as
your home.”"}, {"paragraph": 29, "text": "“Thank you, sir, it’s awfully decent of you.”"}, {"paragraph": 30, "text": "“Where’s this young lady I’ve been hearing such a lot about?”"}, {"paragraph": 31, "text": "Tommy introduced Tuppence."}, {"paragraph": 32, "text": "“Ha!” said Sir William, eyeing her. “Girls aren’t what they used to be
in my young days.”"}, {"paragraph": 33, "text": "“Yes, they are,” said Tuppence. “Their clothes are different, perhaps,
but they themselves are just the same.”"}, {"paragraph": 34, "text": "“Well, perhaps you’re right. Minxes then--minxes now!”"}, {"paragraph": 35, "text": "“That’s it,” said Tuppence. “I’m a frightful minx myself.”"}, {"paragraph": 36, "text": "“I believe you,” said the old gentleman, chuckling, and pinched her ear
in high good-humour. Most young women were terrified of the “old bear,”
 as they termed him. Tuppence’s pertness delighted the old misogynist."}, {"paragraph": 37, "text": "Then came the timid archdeacon, a little bewildered by the company in
which he found himself, glad that his daughter was considered to have
distinguished herself, but unable to help glancing at her from time
to time with nervous apprehension. But Tuppence behaved admirably. She
forbore to cross her legs, set a guard upon her tongue, and steadfastly
refused to smoke."}, {"paragraph": 38, "text": "Dr. Hall came next, and he was followed by the American Ambassador."}, {"paragraph": 39, "text": "“We might as well sit down,” said Julius, when he had introduced all his
guests to each other. “Tuppence, will you----”"}, {"paragraph": 40, "text": "He indicated the place of honour with a wave of his hand."}, {"paragraph": 41, "text": "But Tuppence shook her head."}, {"paragraph": 42, "text": "“No--that’s Jane’s place! When one thinks of how she’s held out all
these years, she ought to be made the queen of the feast to-night.”"}, {"paragraph": 43, "text": "Julius flung her a grateful glance, and Jane came forward shyly to the
allotted seat. Beautiful as she had seemed before, it was as nothing to
the loveliness that now went fully adorned. Tuppence had performed her
part faithfully. The model gown supplied by a famous dressmaker had been
entitled “A tiger lily.” It was all golds and reds and browns, and out
of it rose the pure column of the girl’s white throat, and the bronze
masses of hair that crowned her lovely head. There was admiration in
every eye, as she took her seat."}, {"paragraph": 44, "text": "Soon the supper party was in full swing, and with one accord Tommy was
called upon for a full and complete explanation."}, {"paragraph": 45, "text": "“You’ve been too darned close about the whole business,” Julius accused
him. “You let on to me that you were off to the Argentine--though I
guess you had your reasons for that. The idea of both you and Tuppence
casting me for the part of Mr. Brown just tickles me to death!”"}, {"paragraph": 46, "text": "“The idea was not original to them,” said Mr. Carter gravely. “It was
suggested, and the poison very carefully instilled, by a past-master in
the art. The paragraph in the New York paper suggested the plan to him,
and by means of it he wove a web that nearly enmeshed you fatally.”"}, {"paragraph": 47, "text": "“I never liked him,” said Julius. “I felt from the first that there was
something wrong about him, and I always suspected that it was he who
silenced Mrs. Vandemeyer so appositely. But it wasn’t till I heard that
the order for Tommy’s execution came right on the heels of our interview
with him that Sunday that I began to tumble to the fact that he was the
big bug himself.”"}, {"paragraph": 48, "text": "“I never suspected it at all,” lamented Tuppence. “I’ve always thought
I was so much cleverer than Tommy--but he’s undoubtedly scored over me
handsomely.”"}, {"paragraph": 49, "text": "Julius agreed."}, {"paragraph": 50, "text": "“Tommy’s been the goods this trip! And, instead of sitting there as dumb
as a fish, let him banish his blushes, and tell us all about it.”"}, {"paragraph": 51, "text": "“Hear! hear!”"}, {"paragraph": 52, "text": "“There’s nothing to tell,” said Tommy, acutely uncomfortable. “I was an
awful mug--right up to the time I found that photograph of Annette, and
realized that she was Jane Finn. Then I remembered how persistently she
had shouted out that word ‘Marguerite’--and I thought of the pictures,
and--well, that’s that. Then of course I went over the whole thing to
see where I’d made an ass of myself.”"}, {"paragraph": 53, "text": "“Go on,” said Mr. Carter, as Tommy showed signs of taking refuge in
silence once more."}, {"paragraph": 54, "text": "“That business about Mrs. Vandemeyer had worried me when Julius told me
about it. On the face of it, it seemed that he or Sir James must have
done the trick. But I didn’t know which. Finding that photograph in the
drawer, after that story of how it had been got from him by Inspector
Brown, made me suspect Julius. Then I remembered that it was Sir James
who had discovered the false Jane Finn. In the end, I couldn’t make up
my mind--and just decided to take no chances either way. I left a note
for Julius, in case he was Mr. Brown, saying I was off to the Argentine,
and I dropped Sir James’s letter with the offer of the job by the desk
so that he would see it was a genuine stunt. Then I wrote my letter to
Mr. Carter and rang up Sir James. Taking him into my confidence would
be the best thing either way, so I told him everything except where I
believed the papers to be hidden. The way he helped me to get on the
track of Tuppence and Annette almost disarmed me, but not quite. I kept
my mind open between the two of them. And then I got a bogus note from
Tuppence--and I knew!”"}, {"paragraph": 55, "text": "“But how?”"}, {"paragraph": 56, "text": "Tommy took the note in question from his pocket and passed it round the
table."}, {"paragraph": 57, "text": "“It’s her handwriting all right, but I knew it wasn’t from her because
